sections.h2: Who bills property tax on a Knoxville house?
sections.html:
Two governments send a bill, and the Knox County Property Assessor sets the value behind both. A house inside the city limits owes Knox County tax and City of Knoxville tax, each collected by a different office. Keep the two bills separate, because the city says plainly that payments sent to the wrong office cause errors.

  • City bill: the City of Knoxville Revenue Office, phone 865-215-2084, Suite 453 of the City County Building at 400 Main Street, open weekdays, 8:00 to 4:30. Mail goes to P.O. Box 15001, Knoxville, TN 37901-5001.
  • County bill: the Knox County Trustee, phone 865-215-2305, Suite 427 of the same building, with matching weekday hours. Mail goes to P.O. Box 70, Knoxville, TN 37901, and the Trustee runs six locations.
  • Value questions: the Knox County Property Assessor, 865-215-2360.
  • Deed questions: the Register of Deeds, 865-215-2330.

The city's property tax page lists these contacts side by side, and the county's Trustee page covers the county side.

sections.h2: What is Knoxville like, and how does it affect a sale?
sections.html:
Knoxville sits in the Tennessee Valley, roughly halfway between the Great Smoky Mountains and the Cumberland Plateau. James White founded the town in 1791, and it was incorporated in 1815. The city covers 104.2 square miles, about 98.5 of them land, and the Tennessee River runs through downtown as part of Fort Loudoun Lake after the Holston and French Broad rivers meet in the southeast.

Ridges give the city its shape. Elevations run from just over 800 feet along the riverfront to more than 1,000 feet on West Knoxville hilltops, with Sharp's Ridge in North Knoxville reaching 1,391 feet. The climate is humid subtropical, with just under 52 inches of precipitation a year and about 36 days at or above 90 degrees. Summers are hot and humid.

The housing stock follows the city's growth. Fourth and Gill, Parkridge and Fort Sanders grew up along the old streetcar lines and hold many Victorian and bungalow houses. Sequoyah Hills and Lindbergh Forest were early automobile suburbs with 1920s and 1930s styles. Bearden and Fountain City joined the city when it annexed them in 1962. Knox County Schools runs the public schools, with 89 schools according to Wikipedia, and the University of Tennessee's flagship campus is a steady source of renters and buyers. TVA, Pilot Flying J and the Discovery media networks have a base in the city, and I-40, I-75, I-640, I-275 and the Pellissippi Parkway (I-140) tie it together.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Knoxville city:

  • Estimated population on July 1, 2025: 202,021, up 6.0% from the 2020 base
  • Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 2024: 46.6%, so most households rent
  • Typical owner-occupied house, by value: $239,700
  • Median gross rent: $1,191, with 86,263 households
  • Mean commute: 20.2 minutes

sections.h2: How is a Knoxville property tax bill figured?
sections.html:
The assessor appraises the property, applies a percentage set by use, and the taxing bodies multiply that assessed figure by their rates per $100. The assessor's guide lists the percentages: 25 percent for residential and farm property, 40 percent for commercial and industrial, 30 percent for business personal property and 55 percent for public utilities. A house appraised at $100,000 therefore carries an assessed value of $25,000.

Knox County follows a two-year reappraisal cycle, so values are reset more often here than in counties on a longer cycle. In between, the assessor adds new construction and reviews part of the county each year. An Assessment Change Notice has to go out when a value or classification changes. The county commission and city council set the rates, not the assessor, and the city says it does not appraise anything itself.

Current city and county rates are not listed here, since they change with the budget. Ask the Revenue Office for the city rate and the Trustee for the county rate, or read both off the most recent bill for the parcel.

sections.h2: When is Knoxville property tax due, and is the discount still open?
sections.html:
City tax is due October 1 and turns delinquent on March 1 of the following year. Once March 1 passes, the city adds penalty and interest of 1 percent each per month.

The discount applies only to real estate tax, never to personal property or public utility tax. The city also applies each payment to the oldest unpaid year first, so a delinquent balance from a prior year absorbs money meant for the current bill. The Trustee takes county payments in person, online at propertytax.knoxcountytn.gov, by phone at 865-215-2305 option 3, or by mail. Its software vendor charges 2.5% on a credit card and $1.00 on an e-check, and the city's online payment fees likewise go to its vendor and not to the city.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Knoxville assessment?
sections.html:
Begin with an informal talk with the assessor at 865-215-2360, then go to the county's equalization board if that fails. The assessor lists three valid grounds: your value is too high, another owner's value is too low, or the classification is wrong, such as commercial listed as residential. The amount of tax is never a ground, since the rate is not the assessor's decision.

The county board meets beginning June 1. A disputed assessment generally has to go there first or it becomes final. From the county board you can appeal to the State Board of Equalization by August 1 or within 45 days of the date the county board's notice was sent, whichever is later. The state board starts with a hearing before an administrative judge, who issues a decision within 90 days of the hearing. A taxpayer who still disagrees can petition a chancery court within 60 days after the state board's order becomes final. The Comptroller's appeals page walks through each step. This year's June window is closed, so an owner who missed it should wait for the next tax year's notice cycle.

sections.h2: What tax relief can a Knoxville homeowner claim?
sections.html:
The Trustee's relief page lists a state credit and a freeze. The credit pays part of the bill. It is not an exemption, so the full bill still arrives and the owner pays it.

  • Elderly and disabled homeowners: up to $85 for 2026, with combined 2025 income for all owners capped at $38,470.
  • Disabled veterans and their widows or widowers: up to $444, with no income limit, for an owner whose service-connected rating is permanent and total.
  • Senior freeze: owners 65 or older by December 31, 2026 can freeze the base tax on one home and up to five acres, with a 2025 income cap of $63,470 that counts VA income.

Each program needs a yearly application, and the Assessor's site gives April 5 as the apply-by date. The city's Revenue Office at 865-215-2084 also answers relief questions for city tax.

sections.h2: What happens to tax when a Knoxville house sells?
sections.html:
Tax stays with the house, whatever the contract says. The city states that unpaid tax becomes the new owner's obligation even when the seller agreed to pay it, and that private agreements do not change the city's right to collect. A buyer should ask the Revenue Office for the bill on the parcel, and a seller who owes back tax should get the payoff figure early, from both the city and the Trustee.

Prorating is a matter between the buyer and seller, usually handled by the title company at closing. A seller with a balance, a pending appeal or an inherited house to clear can ask the title company how each item will appear on the settlement statement. Tennessee also holds tax sales for delinquent parcels: the Trustee's page shows a June 2, 2026 sale at the Grande Event Center on Clinton Highway, where bidders had to be current on their own taxes. Clearing an old balance before listing keeps a Knoxville house out of that process.

faqs.q: Does the City of Knoxville collect the same tax as Knox County?
faqs.a: No, they are two separate taxes. The city bills its own rate through the Revenue Office and the county bills its rate through the Trustee. A house inside city limits normally receives both bills, and each office has its own phone number and payment address.

faqs.q: Can I still get the Knoxville city discount this year?
faqs.a: No. The full amount is due now, and delinquency begins March 1 of next year.

faqs.q: Who should I call if my Knoxville assessment looks too high?
faqs.a: Call the Knox County Property Assessor at 865-215-2360 for an informal review. That conversation is not an appeal, so to keep your rights, file with the county's equalization board, which sits beginning June 1.

faqs.q: Will a buyer owe my unpaid Knoxville tax?
faqs.a: Yes, the lien follows the property. The city says unpaid tax becomes the new owner's obligation even if the seller promised to pay, so a title company usually collects any balance from your proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: How do I find out whether I qualify for relief on a Knoxville home?
faqs.a: Check the Trustee's relief page or call the Trustee at 865-215-2305. You must own the home and live in it, and income limits apply to the elderly and disabled credit and to the senior freeze. Applications are due by April 5.
